q: 101. Timber flooring is preferred in ..........
explain: Timber flooring is preferred for auditoriums and dancing halls because it is resilient, provides good acoustics, and offers a comfortable surface for movement.

q: 102. The most commonly used flooring in residential and public buildings is ..........
explain: Cement concrete flooring is the most common due to its durability, ease of construction, and relatively low cost compared to marble or mosaic.

q: 103. In flat slab floor, the flared portion of the columns just below the slab is called ..........
explain: The column capital is the flared top of a column in flat slab construction, designed to increase the shear resistance of the slab.

q: 104. The biggest disadvantages of brick flooring is that ..........
explain: Bricks are porous by nature; therefore, brick flooring tends to absorb water and moisture, which can lead to dampness.

q: 105. Glass flooring is generally preferred when ..........
options: light is to be transmitted from upper to lower floor
explain: Glass flooring (using structural glass blocks) is specifically used to allow natural or artificial light to pass through to the floor below.

q: 106. Flooring used in bath rooms and kitchens of posh residential buildings is ..........
explain: Marble flooring is used in high-end (posh) buildings for its superior aesthetic appeal, cleanliness, and durability in wet areas.

q: 107. The disadvantage of jack arch floor is ..........
options: the ceiling of the floor is not plain from below
extra tie rods are required in the end spans to withstand lateral thrust due to arch action
the joints are susceptible for corrosion
explain: Jack arch floors are outdated because they result in a curved ceiling, require tie rods to handle thrust, and the exposed steel joists can corrode.

q: 108. Terrazzo flooring is obtained ..........
options: by using marble chips as aggregate in concrete
by spreading the marble chips over ordinary wet concrete
by mixing marble powder in ordinary concrete
explain: Terrazzo consists of a mixture of cement and marble chips spread over a concrete base, which is then ground and polished.

q: 109. The oxalic acid is spread and rubbed over the floor which has been ground with machine ..........
options: to make the floor surface look smooth and uniform
to fill up any dents that are left on the floor surface
to make the surface appear glossy
explain: Oxalic acid is used during the final polishing stage of terrazzo or mosaic flooring to react chemically and produce a high-gloss finish.

q: 110. The joints provided in wooden floors are of ..........
explain: Tongue and groove joints are standard for wooden flooring to ensure the boards lock together tightly and prevent gaps or unevenness.

q: 111. The bearing of the lintel should be ..........
explain: The bearing should be at least 10 cm, the height of the lintel, or 1/10 to 1/12 of the span—whichever is greater (though the key indicates minimum, standard practice seeks the safest value).

q: 112. Arches over openings are preferred to lintel beams when ..........
options: loads are heavy and span is large
explain: Arches are used for their aesthetic value, their ability to span larger distances by carrying loads in compression, and provided the supports (abutments) can resist the thrust.

q: 113. The upper horizontal portion of the step where the foot is placed while ascending or descending is known as ..........
explain: The tread is the flat horizontal surface of a stair step that you walk on.

q: 114. Brick lintels are used when the span is ..........
explain: Brick lintels are weak in tension and are only suitable for small openings, typically less than 1 meter.

q: 115. The advantage of R.C.C. lintel is that ..........
options: the sunshade can be cast monolithic along with lintel
there is no limitation on span
they are strong and fire resistant
explain: RCC lintels are versatile; they allow for integrated sunshades (chajjas), are fireproof, and can be designed for various spans.

q: 116. The inner curve of an arch is known as ..........
explain: The intrados is the lower or inner curve of an arch. The underside surface itself is often called the soffit.

q: 117. The wedge shaped units of masonry forming an arch are called ..........
explain: Voussoirs are the individual wedge-shaped blocks (stones or bricks) that make up the body of an arch.

q: 118. Spandril is ..........
options: the curved space formed between the extrados and the horizontal line through the crown
the space in the form of a sector between the intrados and the center of the arch
the curved space between the intrados and springing line
explain: A spandril is the triangular-like space between the outer curve (extrados) of an arch and a rectangular enclosure or horizontal line.

q: 119. The highest point on the extrados of the arch is known as ..........
explain: The crown is the highest part or apex of the arch's exterior curve.

q: 120. The voussoirs fixed at the crown of the arch is called ..........
explain: The 'key' or 'keystone' is the central voussoir at the top of the arch that locks all other pieces into place.

q: 121. A row of arches in continuation is called ..........
explain: An arcade is a succession of arches, each spanning an opening and supported by columns or piers.

q: 122. The points from which the curve of arch springs at the supports are called ..........
explain: Springing points are the specific points where the arch begins to curve away from the support.

q: 123. The inclined surface on the abutment which acts as a seat for the arch is known as ..........
explain: The skewback is the sloped surface on the abutment from which the arch units start their curve.

q: 124. The rise of the arch is defined as the clear vertical distance between ..........
options: the springing line and the highest point on extrados
the springing line and the highest point on intrados
the center of the arch and the crown of the arch
explain: Rise is measured vertically from the horizontal line connecting the springing points (springing line) to the highest point of the intrados.

q: 125. An arch which is formed by two arcs of circles meeting at the apex point is known as ..........
explain: Pointed arches consist of two intersecting curves, typical in Gothic architecture.

q: 126. In a pointed arch if the apex point and the springing points become corners of an isosceles triangle, then it is known as ..........
explain: A lancet arch is a narrow, tall pointed arch where the height is much greater than the width.

q: 127. The pointed arch in which the depth is more at the crown than at the springing is known as ..........
explain: In a variable depth arch, the thickness of the arch rings changes throughout its span, usually being thicker at the crown.

q: 128. If the center of the arch lies on the springing line, it is ..........
explain: A semi-circular arch has its center exactly on the line connecting the two springing points.

q: 129. If the center of the arch lies above the springing line, it is ..........
explain: In a horse-shoe arch, the curve continues past the semi-circle, meaning the center is above the line where it starts curving inward.

q: 130. If the center of the arch lies below the springing line, it is ..........
explain: A segmental arch is less than a semi-circle, meaning its center point is located below the springing line.

q: 131. An arch in the form of a perfect circle used for circular windows is called ..........
explain: A bull's eye arch is a complete 360-degree circular arch often used for aesthetic ventilation or windows.

q: 132. An arch which is constructed either on a flat arch or on a wooden lintel to provide greater strength is called ..........
explain: A relieving arch is built above a lintel or flat arch to divert the weight of the wall above to the side supports.

q: 133. The angle of the skew-back with the horizontal in the case of flat arches is usually ..........
explain: For flat arches, the skewback is typically cut at a 60-degree angle to the horizontal to create a stable base for the compression units.

q: 134. The portion of the wall which supports an arch is termed as ..........
explain: The abutment is the end support of an arch that resists both the vertical load and the horizontal thrust.

q: 135. The lower half of the arch between the crown and the skew-back is known as ..........
explain: The haunch is the section of the arch located roughly halfway between the springing point (skewback) and the crown.

q: 136. The vertical distance between the tops of two successive treads is called ..........
explain: Rise is the vertical height of a single step in a staircase.

q: 137. The projected portion of the tread (which is usually rounded) beyond the face of the riser is ..........
explain: The nosing is the edge of the tread that sticks out over the riser to provide more foot space and safety.

q: 138. A vertical member supporting the hand rail is known as ..........
explain: Balusters are the small vertical pillars that support the handrail of a staircase.

q: 139. A continuous series of steps between landings is called ..........
explain: A flight is an uninterrupted sequence of steps between two floor levels or landings.

q: 140. A level platform at the top or bottom of a flight between the floors is known as ..........
explain: A landing provides a place to rest or change direction in a staircase.

q: 141. A vertical member placed at the ends of flights connecting the hand rail is termed as ..........
explain: The newel post is the sturdy vertical post at the start, end, or turn of a staircase handrail.

q: 142. A group of tapering steps radiating from same point is known as ..........
explain: Winders are steps that are narrower at one end than the other, used to change the direction of the stairs.

q: 143. In domestic buildings, the sufficient width of the stair is about ..........
explain: For residential (domestic) use, a width of 0.9 m (90 cm) is considered sufficient for one person to use comfortably.

q: 144. In public buildings the width of the steps may be kept between ..........
explain: Public buildings require wider stairs for mass egress, typically ranging from 1.5 m to 1.8 m.

q: 145. Normally the rise of the steps would be between ..........
explain: A rise of 10-15 cm is standard for public buildings, while 15-18 cm is common for residential; 10-15 cm is generally safer and more comfortable.

q: 146. The normal tread length varies between ..........
explain: A tread (going) of 25-30 cm is the standard range to accommodate an average adult foot size.

q: 147. Spiral stair is used when ..........
options: architectural appearance is to be improved
the cost of the stair is to be minimized
explain: Spiral stairs are circular in plan and are highly efficient in saving floor space.

q: 148. A stair in which all the steps are winders is ..........
explain: In a spiral stair, every step is a winder radiating from a central post.

q: 149. A stair which changes its direction by 180° is ..........
explain: A half-turn stair (like dog-legged or open newel) reverses direction by 180 degrees.

q: 150. Bifurcated stair is commonly used ..........
options: at the entrance of public buildings
as an emergency stair at the back of the buildings
explain: Bifurcated stairs have a wide initial flight that splits into two narrower flights; they are grand and suitable for public building entrances.

q: 151. When stone slabs are used for risers and treads they are connected by ..........
explain: Stone steps are typically either solid masonry or built as independent slabs supported by walls; they are generally not connected by dowels or scotia in standard construction.

q: 152. Dog-legged stair is a ..........
explain: A dog-legged stair is a type of half-turn stair where the two flights run in opposite directions with no space (well) between them.

q: 153. In a stair, when rise and going are expressed in cms, their sum should be between ..........
explain: A common rule of thumb for comfortable stair design is that the sum of the rise and the going (tread) should be approximately 40 cm to 45 cm.

q: 154. When expressed in cms, the product of rise and going in a stair should be between ..........
explain: For an ergonomic stair, the product of the rise and the going (in cm) is often kept between 400 and 450 (e.g., 15 cm x 28 cm = 420).

q: 155. Lift becomes essential in building when the number of floors exceeds ..........
explain: In standard building bylaws, a lift is generally required when a building is G+3 (4 floors) or higher to ensure accessibility.

q: 156. The pitch or slope of the stair, for comfortable ascent and descent, should be between ..........
explain: A stair slope between 30° and 45° is considered safe and comfortable. Slopes steeper than 45° are too difficult to climb.

q: 157. Approximately triangular-shaped stones used as steps are called ..........
explain: Monoblock steps are solid, single-piece steps, often cut into triangular or rectangular blocks for masonry stairs.

q: 158. How many treads would be there in a straight stair connecting two floors with height difference of 3.6 m? The rise of the steps in 15 cm ..........
explain: Number of risers = 360 cm / 15 cm = 24. For a straight flight, number of treads = risers - 1 = 23 (However, the key indicates 24, which implies the landing is counted as a tread).

q: 159. How many treads would be there in a dog-legged stair connecting two floors with height difference of 3.6 m? The rise of the steps in 15 cm ..........
explain: Similar to Q158, total risers = 24. The total number of treads is often calculated as risers - 1 for the whole stair length excluding landings.

q: 160. A roof which slopes in all the four directions is ..........
explain: A hip roof has slopes on all four sides, which meet at the top to form a ridge.

q: 161. A roof which slopes in two directions is known as ..........
explain: A gable roof (or pitched roof) consists of two sloping surfaces meeting at a ridge, forming a triangle (gable) at the end walls.

q: 162. A roof which slopes in two directions and with a break in each slope is known as ..........
explain: A gambrel roof is similar to a gable roof but each side has two different slopes, with the lower slope being steeper.

q: 163. A roof which slopes in all the four directions and having flat top is known as ..........
explain: A deck roof is a hip roof where the top portion is flat instead of ending in a ridge.

q: 164. A roof which slopes in all four directions and with a break in each slope is known as ..........
explain: A mansard roof is a four-sided gambrel-style hip roof where each side has two slopes, providing extra room in the attic.

q: 165. The horizontal wooden member at the apex of the roof supporting the common rafter is known as ..........
explain: The ridge piece (or ridge board) is the horizontal timber at the very peak of the roof where the upper ends of rafters are fixed.

q: 166. The horizontal wooden or steel members which support the common rafter in a truss are called ..........
explain: Purlins are horizontal members that span across the trusses to support the common rafters or roof sheets.

q: 167. The limiting span of a couple roof is about ..........
explain: A couple roof consists of two rafters meeting at a ridge; it is limited to spans of about 3.5 m because the rafters tend to spread outward under load.

q: 168. In king post truss there will be ..........
explain: A king post truss has a single central vertical post that connects the apex to the tie beam.

q: 169. The number of vertical posts in a queen post truss is ..........
explain: A queen post truss uses two vertical posts to support the rafters, allowing for a larger span than a king post truss.

q: 170. Lean to roof is used generally ..........
explain: Lean-to roofs slope in only one direction and are simplest for narrow structures like sheds, verandahs, or side additions.

q: 171. Queen-post trusses are used when the span is ..........
explain: Queen post trusses are suitable for spans ranging from 8 to 12 meters.

q: 172. Combination of king-post truss and queen post truss is used when the span is ..........
explain: For spans greater than 12 meters, combined trusses or steel trusses are used to provide adequate structural support.

q: 173. A truss is called a composite truss when it ..........
options: has two slopes on each side
is a combination of king and queen post-trusses
is made of two different materials
explain: A composite truss uses two different materials, typically timber for compression members and steel/wrought iron for tension members.

q: 174. Steel trusses have almost replaced the timber trusses because ..........
options: they can be used for large spans
they are more economical than timber and easy to fabricate
they are fire-proof, more strong and permanent
explain: Steel trusses offer superior strength, durability, and fire resistance, and are more cost-effective for industrial or large-scale construction.

q: 175. When more lighting is required inside the buildings such as workshops and factories with fairly large spans ..........
explain: North-light roofs have a steep glazed side facing north to provide uniform, glare-free natural light into large floor areas.

q: 176. The material commonly used to cover the pitched roofs with steel trusses is ..........
options: thatched covering of reed or straw
explain: A.C. sheets (Asbestos Cement) or CGI sheets are the standard choice for covering industrial steel trusses due to their light weight and durability.

q: 177. The desired slope in Madras-terrace roofing is obtained by ..........
options: using varying thickness of brick bat concreting
using varying mortar thickness while laying flat tiles
adjusting the height of the furring piece at the centre
explain: In Madras-terrace roofs, timber furring pieces of varying heights are placed on the joists to create the necessary slope for drainage.

q: 178. Joining two wooden members at an angle is known as ..........
explain: Mitring is the process of joining two pieces of wood at an angle, usually 45 degrees, to form a corner (like a picture frame).

q: 179. A semi-circular moulding provided on the edges of wood is known as ..........
explain: Beading is a decorative semi-circular strip or moulding used to finish edges or joints in woodwork.

q: 180. When a member is subjected to both compression and tension, the type of lengthening joint to be used is ..........
explain: A tabled joint is a scarf joint where the two pieces are notched to interlock, making it strong in both tension and compression.

q: 181. The joint commonly used in wooden trusses where struts and ties meet ..........
explain: A bridle joint is used at the junction of rafters and tie beams or struts in timber trusses for strong, angled connections.

q: 182. The tool normally used by carpenters to plane the surface ..........
explain: The jack plane is the general-purpose plane used for initial smoothing and reducing the thickness of timber.

q: 183. The tool used for cutting small moulding along the edges ..........
explain: A rebate (or rabbet) plane is designed to cut rectangular grooves or recesses along the edges of wooden members.

q: 184. In doors and windows, style is ..........
options: the vertical member of the frame
the vertical member of the shutter
the member which divides the frame into vertical portions
explain: Styles are the outermost vertical members of a door or window shutter.

q: 185. The horizontal members of the shutter of a door or window are called ..........
explain: Rails are the horizontal members that connect the styles in a door or window shutter (top rail, lock rail, bottom rail).

q: 186. The horizontal members of the frame which divides the window horizontally is ..........
explain: A transom is the horizontal member of a frame that separates a door from a window above it or divides a window horizontally.

q: 187. A vertical member of the frame which divides the window vertically is ..........
explain: A mullion is the vertical member of a frame that divides the window into two or more separate lights or shutters.

q: 188. The dimensions of a door or window frame are measured ..........
options: outer to outer on vertical side and inner to inner on the other side
outer to outer on vertical side and outer to outer on both sides
inner to inner on both sides
explain: Door/window sizes are typically specified by the external dimensions of the frame to fit the masonry opening.

q: 189. The normal height of the door in residential buildings ..........
explain: The standard height for a residential door is 2.0 m to 2.1 m.

q: 190. The door designated as 10 DT 20 means ..........
options: a single shuttered door of 1 m x 2 m
a double shuttered door of 1 m x 2 m
a single shuttered door of 2 m x 1 m
a double shuttered door of 2 m x 1 m
explain: In code designation: 10 refers to width (10 dm = 1 m), DT refers to Double Shutter, and 20 refers to height (20 dm = 2 m).

q: 191. The depression on the recess made inside the door frame to receive the shutter is called ..........
explain: A rebate is the continuous step or groove cut into the frame into which the shutter fits when closed.

q: 192. The sill of window in residential buildings is generally kept above the floor level by ..........
explain: Window sill height is usually kept at 75-90 cm from the floor to align with table/desk height and provide safety.

q: 193. A door in which the shutter is formed by joining the vertical wooden boards side by side with tongue and grooved joints and which are fixed together by horizontal supports is called ..........
explain: Battened and ledged doors consist of vertical boards (battens) held together by horizontal members (ledges).

q: 194. In the battened and ledged door, the vertical wooden boards are called ..........
explain: Battens are the vertical boards that form the face of the shutter in a battened door.

q: 195. In the battened and ledged door, the horizontal wooden boards holding the battens together are called ..........
explain: Ledges are the horizontal wooden members to which the vertical battens are secured.

q: 196. The inclined wooden boards which provide additional strength to battens in the battened and ledged door are called ..........
explain: Braces are diagonal members used between ledges to prevent the door from sagging (making it a 'Battened, Ledged, and Braced' door).

q: 197. The type of door used when good lighting is to be permitted into the room ..........
explain: Sash doors (or glazed doors) contain glass panels to allow light transmission while providing a closure.

q: 198. The type of door used when good ventilation is required in the room and at the same time privacy is maintained ..........
explain: Louvered doors have inclined slats (louvers) that allow air to pass through while blocking the line of sight for privacy.

q: 199. The type of door commonly used for garages, shops, and godowns ..........
explain: Rolling shutter doors are made of interlocking steel slats that roll up, providing high security and space efficiency for commercial use.

q: 200. The window in which the shutters can rotate either horizontally or vertically ..........
explain: Pivoted windows have shutters that swing on pivots fixed at the center (either top/bottom or sides), allowing rotation for ventilation.
